title: Why Money Works
subject: econ
paras: Long before coins existed, people traded goods directly. A farmer with extra grain might exchange it for a pair of shoes. This system, called barter, has a serious weakness. The farmer must find a shoemaker who wants grain at the same moment the farmer wants shoes. Economists call this the problem of the "double coincidence of wants."

Money solves this problem by acting as a medium of exchange. The farmer can sell grain to anyone who has money and later use that money to buy shoes from anyone who sells them. The two trades no longer need to happen together or with the same person.

Money also serves as a unit of account, a common measure of value. Without money, a market would need a separate price for every pair of goods: how many fish equal one chicken, how many chickens equal one blanket, and so on. With money, every good needs only one price.

Finally, money is a store of value. Grain can rot and animals can die, but money can be saved and spent later. For this reason, societies have often chosen things that last, such as shells, metal, or salt, as early forms of money.

Today most money is not gold or silver. Paper bills and bank balances have value mainly because people trust that others will accept them. If that trust disappears, for example when prices rise very quickly, money can lose much of its usefulness.

opts: Goods are too heavy to carry.
Each trader must find someone who wants exactly what they offer at the right time.
Farmers do not grow enough grain.
Shoes are more valuable than grain.
